newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST-S.African May CPI, M3, credit seen lower.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-S.African May CPI, M3, credit seen lower.

text.p: * May CPI seen at 9.8 pct y/y from 9.9 pct in April, mainly due to low year-ago base. Monthly pressures relatively benign.

* M3 growth seen up 15.19 pct y/y from 15.44. Telkom inflows offset by rise in govt deposits, fall in notes and coins. Credit growth seen slowing to 16.56 pct y/y from 16.95. Evidence of slowdown in consumer spending main reason.
* Trade balance expected to show 850 million rand surplus, helped by manufacturing exports.
By Paul Richardson

A bevy of indicators out next week are likely to confirm the South African economy is on track for an interest rate cut later this year, barring a major upheaval in the wake of the July 1 exchange control relaxations.

A Reuters consensus poll of economists predicts inflation, money supply and private sector credit extension -- three of the main factors cited by Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals for his reluctance to cut interest rates -- will all have eased in May.
The June 19 Quarterly Bulletin suggested the central bank saw no immediate need for a rate cut, but economists remain hopeful of an easing in the third or fourth quarter.
The May consumer price index (CPI) will be released at 0900 GMT on Wednesday.

The poll of 11 economists forecast the year-on-year rate would rise between 9.6 and 10.1 percent, with consensus at 9.8 percent or 0.6 percent month-on-month. Annual inflation in April was 9.9 percent.
Most economists said that inflationary pressures in May were likely to have been benign and that a low base effect would be the main reason for the year-on-year rise.

"From both the demand side and the cost-push side you have a fairly benign environment," said JP Morgan emerging markets economist Peter Worthington, citing a strong rand, cheaper oil, higher productivity and signs of slowing private consumption.

Economists also noted that consumer inflation was likely to have peaked in the month, if not already in April, and that the lagged effect of a sharp drop in the imported component of producer inflation in April could also prevent the CPI from breaching the psychological 10 percent barrier.
Next Friday, the Reserve Bank releases its latest money supply and private sector credit extension data at 1500 GMT.
M3 growth is expected to show a rise of between 14.2 and 16.35 percent, while private sector credit growth is expected to increase by between 16.0 and 16.82 percent.
Consensus on M3 was 15.19 percent and 16.5 percent on private sector from 15.44 and 16.95 respectively in April.

The main influence on money supply would be the inflow of the proceeds of the sale of a strategic equity stake in telecommunications utility Telkom, which resulted in a 5.5 billion rand ($1.26 billion) inflow into the country last month.
This would be offset by an increase in government deposits, a continuing slowdown in notes and coins in circulation, and a slight decline in net reserves, economists said.
"What will also help is that the Reserve Bank probably generated profits on its forward book," an economist added.

Private sector credit was expected to benefit from the slowdown in private consumption expenditure evidenced by a fall in new car sales in May as well as sharp declines in profits at consumer-driven retail companies.
Nedcor economist Kevin Lings noted that further assistance could come from the fact that companies' recent financing of high inventory levels was easing off.

"The consumer is at that point in the credit cycle where he is stretched to the limit and from here onwards I suspect that we are going to see a marked slowdown in credit extension to levels much more in line with guidelines set by the Reserve Bank," Boland Bank economist Francois Jansen said.
"In fact, if it wasn't for the relaxation of exchange controls on July 1, Stals could have been tempted to cut interest rates by one percentage point because all the factors are there."
A Customs and Excise official said that May's trade balance would be released in the latter half of next week.
Those economists prepared to predict the notoriously volatile figure predicted a surplus of 850 million rand from 730 million rand in April.

"The fact that manufacturing production was so strong in April suggests that there was increased production for export. There is normally a time lag between production and export," BOE NatWest economist Nick Barnardt said.
